title: Edison Didn't Invent the Light Bulb. So Who Did?
description: In the autumn of 1881, the first public building in the world lit entirely by electricity was a London theatre. And the bulbs weren't Edison's. This is the story of Joseph Swan, Thomas Edison, and why we remember one name instead of the other.
notes: FACT-CHECK before recording: Savoy Theatre 1881 (first public building lit entirely by electricity, Swan lamps); Davy arc lamp early 1800s; Swan carbon lamp c.1860 and poor vacuum; Sprengel pump / late 1870s; Swan public demos Dec 1878-Feb 1879; Swan's house Gateshead 1880; Edison 13.5 h carbonised cotton thread Oct 22, 1879; Menlo Park public show Dec 31, 1879; high-resistance filament and parallel wiring; 1883 Edison & Swan United Electric Light Company (Ediswan); Pearl Street Station Sept 1882; 'Wizard of Menlo Park'. Tone: neutral, no accusation that Edison stole anything.

scenes.text: In the autumn of eighteen eighty-one, a theatre in London did something no public building in the world had done before. It lit the whole place with electric light. Not gas. Not candles. Over a thousand glowing bulbs. And here's the part nobody tells you: those bulbs were not Thomas Edison's.

If you grew up anywhere in the world, you were probably taught one name for the light bulb. Thomas Edison. But the real story is stranger, and a lot more interesting. It starts decades before either of them.

In the early eighteen hundreds, a chemist named Humphry Davy created a blinding electric arc between two sticks of carbon. It was spectacular. It was also far too fierce for a living room. It belonged on a street corner, not above a dinner table.

The better idea was gentler. Pass electricity through a thin thread until it glows, inside a glass bulb with no air. Inventors chased that idea for decades. But the thread always burned out in seconds, or minutes.

Joseph Swan, a chemist in Newcastle, England, started on this problem in the eighteen-fifties. Around eighteen sixty, he had a working lamp with a strip of carbon. But the vacuum pumps of his day were poor. The bulb blackened, and died quickly. So Swan did what many inventors do. He put it away, and waited for the world to catch up.

The world caught up in the late eighteen-seventies. Better vacuum pumps arrived. Swan went back to his lamps, and by eighteen seventy-eight and seventy-nine, he was showing working bulbs to audiences in Newcastle.

Across the Atlantic, Thomas Edison was running a research lab at Menlo Park, New Jersey. He had investors, a team, and a very big promise: electric light for everyone. But Edison wasn't trying to build just a bulb. He was trying to build a whole system.

The key, his team realised, was a filament with high resistance. That way, each lamp used very little current, and thousands of them could be wired side by side across a city. Without that idea, electric light stays a laboratory trick.

So they tested thousands of materials. Platinum. Paper. Cotton thread. Even bamboo. And on October twenty-second, eighteen seventy-nine, a carbonised cotton thread glowed for around thirteen and a half hours.
On New Year's Eve, eighteen seventy-nine, Edison put on a public show at Menlo Park. Crowds came by train from New York to see lamps glowing with no flame at all. The newspapers loved it.
Meanwhile, back in England, Swan wasn't standing still. In eighteen eighty, he lit his own home in Gateshead with electric bulbs, one of the first houses in the world to glow like that.

Now both men had patents, in different countries. And when Edison's lamps arrived in Britain, Swan was ready. A legal fight loomed. Instead of fighting to the end, in eighteen eighty-three they joined forces, and created one company: the Edison and Swan United Electric Light Company.

So why do we remember Edison? Because Edison didn't stop at the bulb. He built everything around it: generators, wiring, sockets, meters. In September eighteen eighty-two, his Pearl Street power station in Manhattan began selling electricity to customers.

And Edison understood publicity better than almost anyone. Reporters. Demonstrations. A reputation as the Wizard of Menlo Park. Swan was a quiet scientist. Edison was a showman, with a system to sell.
scenes.image: Thomas Edison Wizard of Menlo Park

scenes.text: So who invented the light bulb? Davy showed that electricity could make light. Swan built a working bulb. Edison made it practical, and put it in every home. Credit, in the real world, is rarely one person's.
scenes.image: history of the incandescent light bulb

scenes.text: Remember that London theatre. The first public building in the world lit by electricity glowed with bulbs most people can't name. Because an invention isn't finished when it works. It's finished when it works for everyone.
